title: Decision-making 102
primary_topics: The anatomy of a well-written judicial decision: the five essential parts from Velarde vs Social Justice Society
Credibility assessment as the most crucial element of fact-finding -- trial judges vs appellate courts
Specific requirements for the dispositive portion in criminal and civil cases
sub_topics: Sequel to October 7 column on judicial decision-making as Aristotelian syllogism
Facts: admitted, judicially noticed, or proven by documentary and verbal evidence
Trial judges assess credibility via demeanor on the stand; appellate courts rely only on transcripts
Everyday credibility analogies: crying son vs elder sister; irate wife vs wayward husband
Witness integrity test: capacity to observe, opportunity to know, ability to remember, consistency with common experience
Cross-examination as the best credibility test -- three 'Cs': coherence, consistency, correctness
Affidavits are often one-sided (lawyer-prepared, not by witnesses) -- require searing cross-examination
Velarde vs Social Justice Society (April 28, 2004) -- CJ Panganiban's ponencia -- five-part decision structure
Five essential parts: (1) statement of case; (2) statement of facts; (3) issues/assignment of errors; (4) court ruling; (5) dispositive portion
Optional: prologue (concise summary of facts/issues) and epilogue (summary of key legal principles)
Statement of facts: per-witness summary or per-court evaluation
Court ruling: each issue addressed individually unless intertwined
Criminal case disposition: innocence/guilt, specific crime, penalty, participation, modifying circumstances, civil liability, costs
Acquittal: immediate release order + director of Bureau of Corrections report within 10 days
Civil case disposition: complaint granted or denied, specific relief, costs
Completeness test: parties know rights/obligations; know how to execute; no further proceedings needed; proper relief granted

stances.claim: Credibility assessment is the most crucial dimension of judicial fact-finding: trial judges have the decisive advantage over appellate courts because they observe witnesses on the stand, while appellate courts rely only on cold transcripts — making the trial judge's assessment of demeanor and conduct the least reversible finding.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-competence argument: trial-court primacy in credibility grounded in observational access that appellate courts structurally lack

stances.claim: Cross-examination is the best — and historically unmatched — method for testing witness credibility, especially for lawyer-prepared affidavits that are inherently one-sided; the best trial lawyer is the best cross-examiner, testing coherence, consistency, and correctness.
stances.rhetorical_move: practitioner-wisdom assertion: distilling centuries of trial advocacy into a three-C framework

stances.claim: The five-part Velarde decision structure — statement of case, facts, issues, court ruling, dispositive portion — is the constitutional standard for good decision writing, and the completeness test (parties know rights, know how to execute, no further proceedings needed, proper relief granted) is the operational measure of a valid disposition.
stances.rhetorical_move: self-citation as institutional standard: CJ's own Velarde ponencia as the authoritative template

notable_anecdotes: The everyday credibility analogies — a crying son describing his elder sister's scolding, an irate wife examining lipstick on her husband's shirt — used to bridge the abstract judicial concept of witness credibility assessment to universal human experiences of evaluating truthfulness.

The disclosure that affidavits are 'often prepared by lawyers, not by the witnesses' — making them inherently one-sided and requiring 'searing cross-examination' to expose their constructed nature: a practitioner insight that reveals the gap between the formal appearance of sworn testimony and its actual reliability.

The acquittal-specific disposition requirement — immediate release order plus a mandatory report from the director of the Bureau of Corrections within 10 days on the exact date of release — as a procedural safeguard often overlooked in commentary on judicial decisions, embedded in the five-part framework as an accountability mechanism.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban continues his Decision-making series (sequel to his October 7 column on the Aristotelian syllogism) by focusing on the fact-finding and decision-writing dimensions of judicial decision-making. He argues that witness credibility is the most crucial element of fact-finding: trial judges have a structural advantage over appellate courts because they observe witnesses on the stand while appellate courts rely only on transcripts -- an advantage he illustrates with everyday analogies (a mother hearing her son describe a sibling's scolding; an irate wife examining lipstick marks). He identifies cross-examination -- testing coherence, consistency, and correctness -- as the historically unmatched credibility tool, especially essential for lawyer-prepared affidavits that are inherently one-sided. For decision structure, he draws on his own Velarde vs Social Justice Society ponencia (April 28, 2004) to articulate the five essential parts: statement of the case, statement of facts, issues/assignment of errors, court ruling (each issue addressed separately), and dispositive portion -- with optional prologue and epilogue for high-profile cases. He specifies the content required for criminal dispositions (guilt/innocence, specific crime, penalty, participation, modifying circumstances, civil liability, costs; plus -- for acquittals -- an immediate release order and a mandatory Bureau of Corrections report within 10 days), civil dispositions (relief granted or denied, costs), and the four-part completeness test: parties know their rights and obligations, know how to execute the decision, no further proceedings are needed, and proper relief is granted.
